findings.paper_title: Item 4. DSG Budget Monitoring FY 2026-27 - Oct 2026
findings.headline: Forecast includes £6m Early Years underspend and £1m Schools Block underspend, but paper states these 'do not resolve the underlying High Needs funding gap'

The paper explicitly notes these offsets are insufficient and the priority must be to 'contain future growth through local sufficiency, inclusion, early intervention and robust placement management.'
findings.matters: Shows a broad DSG portfolio where some blocks underspend (often related to take-up volatility) while High Needs overruns massively; offsetting approach cannot be relied upon, requiring structural solutions.

findings.quote: The £6m Early Years underspend and £1m Schools Block underspend provide a significant offset in FY 2026-27, but they do not resolve the underlying High Needs funding gap.

findings.paper_title: Item 4. DSG Budget Monitoring FY 2026-27 - Oct 2026
findings.headline: Post-16 EHCP demand forecast to accelerate, with growth concentrating in the 16-25 age range while school-age demand levels off
findings.detail: While some school-age EHCP cohorts are expected to level off, the 16-25 age range shows continued growth trajectory. Post-16 placements (Further Education and specialist) are typically funded for longer durations and carry higher average costs than school-age placements.
findings.matters: Signals that High Needs cost pressures will persist and likely increase beyond FY 2026-27; the shift to post-16 means longer-duration, higher-cost commitments that compound budget pressure.
findings.figures: Forecast shows continued growth in 16-25 cohort; Further Education forecast to increase by £1.079m; resource bases £0.870m
findings.quote: Forecasts indicate that future EHCP growth is increasingly concentrated within the 16 to 25 age range. Whilst demand across a number of school-age cohorts begins to level off over the medium term, the number of young people requiring post-16 support continues to increase. This will place additional pressure on Further Education provision and specialist post-16 placements, which are typically funded for longer durations and often carry higher average costs than mainstream school placements.

findings.paper_title: Item 4. DSG Budget Monitoring FY 2026-27 - Oct 2026
findings.headline: Mainstream top-up funding forecast to increase by £1.916m, with FTE growing 55% (1,130 vs 729 in 2020-21) despite overall school rolls declining
findings.detail: More pupils are requiring top-up funding in mainstream schools despite falling mainstream rolls, indicating both volume growth and increasing average cost per pupil (£12.7k vs £9.3k). This demonstrates that a larger proportion of the remaining mainstream pupil population requires additional support.
findings.matters: Shows the structural shift is not confined to specialist placements; mainstream settings are also absorbing cost pressures from higher-need cohorts, requiring investment in mainstream capacity and training.
findings.figures: £1.916m increase; 1,130 FTE vs 729 FTE (55% increase); average cost £12.7k vs £9.3k
findings.quote: Mainstream FTE has grown from approximately 729 in FY 2020-21 to 1,130 in FY 2026-27, while the average cost has increased from approximately £9.3k to £12.7k. This demonstrates that, despite falling school rolls, a larger number and proportion of pupils are requiring additional support in mainstream settings.

findings.paper_title: Item 4. DSG Budget Monitoring FY 2026-27 - Oct 2026
findings.headline: Independent specialist placements (£21.047m) are the largest High Needs cost driver, with FTE up 59% (404 vs 254 in 2020-21) and average cost up 51% (£52.0k vs £34.3k)
findings.detail: The £2.979m year-on-year increase reflects both volume growth and significant cost inflation. This is the single largest component of the £23.112m High Needs overspend. The average cost rise from £34.3k to £52.0k suggests both provider cost increases and potential mix shift towards more complex placements.
findings.matters: Large, sustained cost inflation in a demand-led provision type signals a market-wide issue (provider costs, market tightness) rather than a single-council procurement issue; pricing discipline becomes critical.
findings.figures: £21.047m forecast; 404 FTE vs 254 FTE (59% increase); average cost from £34.3k to £52.0k (51% increase)
findings.quote: Independent specialist placements are the largest single year-on-year driver, increasing by £2.979m to £21.047m. The pressure reflects both volume and price: the current forecast supports approximately 404 FTE placements, compared with 254 FTE in FY 2020-21, while the average placement cost has risen from approximately £34.3k to £52.0k.

findings.paper_title: Item 4. DSG Budget Monitoring FY 2026-27 - Oct 2026
findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit forecast to reach £19.368m by 31 March 2027, after an in-year overspend of £16.112m
findings.detail: Brought-forward deficit of £3.255m (working assumption includes 90% write-off through High Needs Stability Grant) plus £16.112m in-year pressure. The paper states the write-off 'does not address the underlying in-year gap between High Needs funding and expenditure' and that 'the continuing rise in the annual High Needs pressure therefore remains the principal risk to the sustainability of the DSG.'
findings.matters: Growing cumulative deficits ultimately draw on general fund reserves; government write-offs do not address structural funding gaps, leaving councils with material medium-term balance sheet pressures.

findings.quote: After the forecast in-year pressure of £16.112m, the cumulative DSG deficit would increase to £19.368m by 31 March 2027 at the current rate.

findings.paper_title: Item 4. DSG Budget Monitoring FY 2026-27 - Oct 2026
findings.headline: EHCP numbers have grown 32.6% since 2021 while school-age population has declined 5.3% (primary) to 3.7% (secondary)
findings.detail: 3,584 EHCPs in August 2026 vs 2,703 in 2021, with the 12-month trailing growth rate accelerating from 0.42% (November 2025) to 0.63% (August 2026). Primary pupils fell from 18,334 to 16,505; secondary from 9,956 to 9,590. This indicates a structural shift: the proportion of pupils requiring specialist support is rising within a shrinking cohort.
findings.matters: Rising complexity and identification of need within a declining population is not cyclical and will not be solved by demographic recovery; it signals permanent changes to funding ratios and service composition.

findings.quote: Despite a declining school-age population, demand for special educational needs and/or disabilities (SEND) support continues to grow. Rising Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCP) numbers, increasing complexity of need and higher specialist placement costs remain the key drivers of expenditure within the High Needs Block.

findings.matters: Doubling of a major budget block in five years, with acceleration rather than stabilisation, indicates a structural trend that will not reverse; councils with similar demographics face similar pressures.

findings.headline: Treasury forecast benefits from internal borrowing capacity and elevated interest rates: £0.688m underspend as external borrowing proves unnecessary and cash interest outperforms budget.
findings.detail: Finance is forecasting net underspend of £0.276m (against a notional budget of -£3.335m), driven by Treasury underspend of £0.688m. The budget had assumed external borrowing as 'the most prudent assumption' but can be met internally, eliminating external interest payments. High interest rates mean cash balance returns exceed budget, and there is 'a possible rate increase in year'. This provides a material offset to service-level overspends.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing capacity extends liquidity runway and reduces near-term refinancing risk; high interest rate benefit is a cyclical tailwind that will reverse if rates fall, so it is not a sustainable offset to structural overspends.
findings.figures: Treasury underspend £0.688m; Finance net underspend £0.276m on budget of -£3.335m
findings.quote: Interest earned on cash balances is therefore expected to be higher than budgeted for.

findings.headline: Coroner's Service (Westminster-managed) overspending £0.636m with no council control; external audit fees up £0.130m from national audit backlog.
findings.detail: Two cost pressures sit outside direct council control. The Coroner's Service, managed by Westminster City Council, is overspending £0.636m due to extra capacity needed to clear case backlog, incurring additional staffing and property costs. External audit fees are £0.130m above budget because 'the system tackles the national audit backlog and build back continues to demand additional audit resource.' Together these represent £0.766m of uncontrollable cost growth.
findings.matters: Uncontrollable cost pressures (shared services, regulatory costs) reduce council leverage over outturn and signal structural issues (audit backlog) beyond individual council control.
findings.figures: Coroner's overspend £0.636m; audit fee pressure £0.130m; combined £0.766m
findings.quote: The Coroner's Service is forecast to overspend by £0.636m. This is a shared service managed by Westminster City Council where extra capacity is needed to clear the backlog of cases, so the service is incurring additional staffing and property costs to achieve this.

findings.headline: HRA £11.7m revenue surplus masks underlying operational pressures: £7.7m overspends in repairs, management, and building safety offset by £5.8m programme slippage.
findings.detail: The HRA is forecasting £11.7m in-year surplus with closing balance of £152.658m, but this is driven by significant offsetting positions: Repairs & Maintenance +£2.9m overspend, General Supervision & Management +£3.7m, Special Supervision +£1.1m, largely offset by External Decorations programme slippage of -£5.8m, depreciation charge -£1.8m, and rental income -£1.8m. Overspends are driven by disrepair, damp and mould remediation, stock condition surveys, building safety surveys, and waking watch costs at Eliot and Wentworth Court.
findings.matters: HRA surplus masks estate condition remediation; slippage indicates either deferred bills or constrained remediation capacity, and both have lender implications for asset quality and future liability.
findings.figures: HRA surplus £11.7m; closing balance £152.658m; Repairs & Maintenance +£2.9m, General Supervision +£3.7m, Special Supervision +£1.1m overspends; External Decorations -£5.8m slippage; depreciation -£1.8m; rental income -£1.8m
findings.quote: Repairs and Maintenance is currently forecasting a +£2.9m overspend, General Supervision and Management is overspending by +£3.7m and Special Supervision and Management is showing a +£1.1m overspend.

findings.headline: National pay award at 3.3% exceeds budget provision of 2.5% by £1.2m; council has 1% inflation sensitivity of £5m per point.
findings.detail: The national local government pay award was finalised in July at 3.3%, exceeding the budget provision of 2.5% and creating £1.2m pressure on the inflation contingency (budgeted at £15.362m for 2.8% expected inflation). The council explicitly states '1% of inflation adding £5.0m to costs', indicating material sensitivity. With interest rates remaining high and 'a possible rate increase in year', the council faces further upside inflation risk.
findings.matters: Pay award slippage and residual inflation sensitivity constrain the plausibility of full-year outturn recovery; a £5m-per-percentage-point sensitivity means 0.5% forecast miss becomes a £2.5m outturn movement.
findings.figures: Pay award 3.3% vs 2.5% budgeted = £1.2m pressure; 1% inflation = £5.0m impact; inflation contingency £15.362m on 2.8% expected inflation
findings.quote: The national local government pay award has been finalised in July at a 3.3% increase. This is not yet reflected in service budgets and is higher than the provision (2.5%) allowed for when the budget was set leading to a pressure on the contingency of £1.2m.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation caseload grew 188 cases in Q1 to 5,005 despite £4.593m mitigation planned; full-year forecast 'subject to substantial risk.'
findings.detail: Housing is forecasting breakeven dependent on £4.593m mitigation, but temporary accommodation demand is accelerating: 188 net new cases in Q1 (5,005 now vs 4,817 at year start). The service acknowledges that 'numbers will not just need to be stabilised but significant net reduction achieved'. Current ratio is 10 new cases entering for every 1 leaving; the ambition is to reverse this to 10 leaving for every 3 entering. The council acknowledges 'changes to the delivery of homelessness services are likely to both take time to implement and deliver an improved financial position', and the forecast 'remains subject to substantial risk.'
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a material and visible demand driver; accelerating caseload in Q1 despite mitigation signals either demand acceleration or fragility of containment assumptions.
findings.figures: Q1 caseload 5,005 vs 4,817 start of year (+188 cases); budget mitigation £4.593m; £0.750m full-year savings achieved on unit rate reductions
findings.quote: Current overall numbers housed in TA or assessed as owed statutory homelessness duty as at the end of Q1 was 5,005 compared to a start of year position of 4,817, a growth of 188 cases.

findings.headline: Children's Services £1.160m net overspend despite £3.179m mitigation, with £5.04m children's social care overspend and £1.9m SEN transport overspend driven by EHCP growth and placement complexity.
findings.detail: Children's forecasts £1.160m net overspend with significant offsetting pressures: £5.04m children's social care overspend (residential placements and homecare), £1.6m year-on-year increase in Supporting Disabled Children, and £1.9m SEN transport overspend from growth in Education, Health and Care Plans and complexity of need. These are partially offset by £3.56m of grant-funded underspends. The forecast carries 'high risk' if service step-down plans (transitions from high-cost to lower-cost placements) do not materialise as planned.
findings.matters: SEND placement demand and complexity are rising nationally; councils reporting effective step-down delivery or struggling to execute it are both visible to sector and lenders as early indicators of broader children's services sustainability.
findings.figures: £1.160m net overspend; £3.179m mitigating actions; £5.04m children's social care overspend; £1.9m SEN transport overspend; £1.6m year-on-year increase Supporting Disabled Children; £3.56m grant-funded offsets
findings.quote: The main pressure areas are not unique to Wandsworth and are predominately linked to rising complexity of need, continued growth in numbers of children with special educational needs and disabilities, and a placements market unable to meet need and demand both locally and nationally.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care demand pressures driving £3.477m Health overspend from unfunded demographic growth and increasing complexity of need.
findings.detail: Health is forecasting £3.477m overspend primarily from Adult Social Care demand in Services for Older People, Sensory and Physical Disabilities, and Learning Disabilities, reflecting 'underlying unfunded demographic growth and increasing complexity of need'. Mitigation of £0.608m relies on working with health partners to align cost responsibility under the Care Act, dependent on assessment outcomes and continued health partner agreement on responsibilities.
findings.matters: Adult social care demand and complexity pressures are now visible to PWLB as a common council risk; unfunded demographic growth is structural and resists both savings and service redesign.
findings.figures: £3.477m overspend on Health budget £122.336m; £0.608m mitigation actions; £1.630m future demand growth forecast (including £1.001m from child-to-adult transition)
findings.quote: This is reflecting underlying unfunded demographic growth and increasing complexity of need, particularly in services for older people and adults with learning disabilities.

findings.headline: General Fund forecast £5.306m overspend (1.7%), dependent on delivery of £12m in mitigating actions; position will 'deteriorate' if mitigations do not land.
findings.detail: The council projects £5.306m overspend on a £311.203m budget 'assuming the in-year delivery of a total of £12m of mitigating actions.' The paper explicitly warns: 'In the event that these mitigations are not delivered, the position may deteriorate beyond the forecast currently reported.' The mitigations are concentrated: Housing £4.6m, Children's £3.2m, Transport £1.3m, Environment £1.1m, and others across services facing structural demand pressures.
findings.matters: A council whose Q1 outturn depends on mitigations not yet delivered carries material risk of a worse full-year position; lenders and peer councils assess whether this reflects delivery capability or forecast optimism.
findings.figures: £5.306m overspend; 1.7% of £311.203m budget; £12m mitigating actions across services; Health £0.608m, Environment £1.099m, Children's £3.179m, Finance £1.133m, Housing £4.593m, Transport £1.290m mitigation
findings.quote: In the event that these mitigations are not delivered, the position may deteriorate beyond the forecast currently reported.

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Appendix A
findings.headline: Consumer Price Index at 3.1% (August 2026) exceeds HRA business plan assumptions of 2.5%-3%, costing £1.3m per 1% overage
findings.detail: Consumer Price Index stood at 3.1% in August 2026, above the HRA business plan's longer-term assumptions of 2.5% for general running costs and pay, and 3% for repairs and maintenance. The business plan assumes inflation will fall back towards the Bank of England target of 2% in the medium term. The cost of each 1% of inflation above assumptions, if not matched by compensating income increases or spending reductions, is approximately £1.3m per annum. This inflation gap is a key driver of the revenue overspends reported in repairs and management.
findings.matters: The gap between planned and actual inflation indicates the business plan's cost assumptions may be optimistic. If inflation remains elevated, the HRA will face continued operating pressure requiring either additional rent increases, efficiency savings, or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: CPI 3.1% (August 2026) vs plan assumption 2.5% general and 3% repairs; cost impact £1.3m per 1% overage
findings.quote: If actual inflation is 1% above these longer term base assumptions (and not matched by a compensating income increase (through rents) or spend reductions elsewhere to balance), the additional cost equates to approximately £1.3m per annum for each additional 1% suffered.

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Appendix A
findings.headline: Rent convergence policy adopted generating additional £0.5m (2027/28) and £1m (2028/29) annual income from affected tenants
findings.detail: From April 2027, the council is implementing a rent convergence policy allowing higher rent increases for tenants currently charged below formula rent. Increases are capped at £1 per week in 2027/28 and £2 per week in 2028/29. The policy would affect approximately 9,900 tenants (60% of tenancies), predominantly in 1 and 2-bedroom properties. Modelling suggests this generates additional income of £0.5m in 2027/28 and £1m in 2028/29, compounding to cumulative benefit of approximately £37m by 2036/37. The policy is designed to support enhanced capital investment in existing stock and reduce long-term borrowing requirements. Implementation is subject to annual decision.
findings.matters: This is a discretionary new revenue source built into the business plan to bridge operating costs and borrowing needs, but its continuation depends on annual political decision. Around 70% of affected tenants receive Housing Benefit or Universal Credit, so the cost is substantially met by government.
findings.figures: 9,900 tenants affected (60%); £0.5m additional income 2027/28; £1m in 2028/29; £37m cumulative by 2036/37
findings.quote: Current modelling suggests that, if applied in full, the introduction of rent convergence would impact up to 9,900 Wandsworth tenants (c.60% of all tenanted properties) in April 2027, generating an additional £0.5m in 2027/28 above the core rent increase, and an additional £1m (£1.5m compounded) in 2028/29. Although, as referenced, the application of convergence would be subject to annual decision, modelling suggests that if applied in full it would generate c.£37m of additional resources by 2036/37

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Appendix A
findings.headline: Building Safety Regulator approval takes median 35 weeks against target of 12 weeks for higher-risk building schemes
findings.detail: Higher-risk building (HRB) schemes within the HRA capital programme are experiencing delays at the Building Safety Regulator's Gateway Two pre-construction approval stage. According to BSR data for April-June 2026, the target approval rate is 12 weeks but the median approval time remains at 35 weeks. This delay is driving cost inflation across schemes, as contractors extend timescales and add resources to meet additional BSR compliance requirements, and as consultants take on Principal Designer roles with greater responsibility. Cost increases depend on the nature and complexity of individual schemes.
findings.matters: Capital scheme delays and cost inflation affect the deliverability of the capital programme and may require re-provisioning if the delays extend. This is a regulatory bottleneck outside the council's direct control.
findings.figures: Target 12-week approval rate; median approval time 35 weeks
findings.quote: According to the BSR, building control approval application data for April to June 2026, schemes have a rolling 12-week approval rate, however the median approval time remains at 35 weeks. Consequently, costs have increased across these schemes with the value of these price upturns being dependent on the nature and complexity of the project.

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Appendix A
findings.headline: Stock condition surveys at 46% completion for tenanted properties against December 2026 regulator deadline
findings.detail: The council committed to the Regulator of Social Housing to complete 100% of stock condition surveys by 31 December 2026, accelerated from the original five-year programme. As of 31 August 2026, only 8,074 tenanted surveys were completed against a target of 17,591 (46%) and 2,089 communal surveys against 2,757 (76%). Progress has slowed and the council is working to re-profile targets with the survey provider. The delayed completion means asset condition data will not be available to inform the 2027/28 capital programme.
findings.matters: This represents a regulatory commitment at risk of non-delivery, with potential implications for the council's relationship with the housing regulator. The delayed asset condition data also means capital programming will be less informed by actual stock condition than planned.
findings.figures: 8,074 of 17,591 tenanted surveys (46%); 2,089 of 2,757 communal surveys (76%) as at 31 August 2026
findings.quote: At the end of August 2026 2,089 communal surveys were completed against a target of 2,757 (76% of total required completed) and 8,074 tenanted surveys were completed against a target of 17,591 (46% of total required completed). Progress has slowed on these surveys, and work is underway to re-profile targets with the provider to ensure this work is delivered.

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Appendix A
findings.headline: Repairs and Maintenance forecasting £2.9m overspend, General Supervision £3.7m, Special Supervision £1.1m in 2026/27
findings.detail: The HRA is forecasting gross overspends totalling £7.7m in 2026/27 across three areas: Repairs and Maintenance (£2.9m), General Supervision and Management (£3.7m), and Special Supervision and Management (£1.1m). The Repairs overspend is primarily driven by disrepair, damp and mould remediation, and remedial works arising from stock condition surveys. The General Management overspend reflects disrepair settlements, legal costs, acceleration of stock condition surveys, building safety surveys, and reinstatement of waking watch at two buildings. These are structural cost pressures, not one-off items.
findings.matters: These overspends indicate that the HRA operating environment is harder than baseline budget, with recurring structural pressures from building safety and asset condition driving costs above plan. This suggests future budgets may face similar pressures.
findings.figures: £2.9m repairs; £3.7m general supervision; £1.1m special supervision
findings.quote: Repairs and Maintenance is currently forecasting a +£2.9m overspend, General Supervision and Management is overspending by +£3.7m and Special Supervision and Management is showing a +£1.1m overspend. This is largely offset by slippage on the External Decorations programme of -£5.8m, lower than anticipated depreciation charge -£1.8m and increased rental income of -£1.8m

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Appendix A
findings.headline: Business plan assumes HRA borrowing at 4.5% average cost against current PWLB rates of 6.60% for 50-year loans
findings.detail: The HRA business plan assumes future borrowing will cost 4.5% on average over its ten-year horizon. Current Public Works Loan Board rates are approximately 6.60% for 50-year loans (6.0% with HRA concessional discount). All borrowing undertaken in 2024/25, 2025/26 and anticipated 2026/27 is being internally funded from General Fund cash reserves specifically because PWLB rates are described as 'higher than the longer term projections assumed within the HRA business plan'. The council is exposed to refinancing risk if external borrowing becomes necessary before PWLB rates fall to planned levels.
findings.matters: The gap between assumed and actual borrowing costs represents embedded financial risk. If rates remain elevated, either the HRA will face higher debt service than planned, or the council will need to make offsetting decisions on rent, capital investment, or reserve draw-down.
findings.figures: Current PWLB rates c.6.60% for 50-year loans; business plan assumption of average 4.5%
findings.quote: Current PWLB rates are c.6.60% for 50-year loans. If the Council uses the PWLB for HRA borrowing it would currently benefit from a concession rate for HRA rate loans which will mean a 0.6% discount from the headline PWLB interest rates... Future assumptions in the HRA business plan are that a significant proportion of the capital programme will need to be financed by borrowing and that debt will be taken on at an average rate of 4.5%. Whilst this is below the currently available rates from the PWLB, and therefore does present a financial risk, the rate has been set as the average cost of borrowing for the purpose of the financial modelling

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Appendix A
findings.headline: Interest and debt repayment forecast to rise from £17m (12% of rental income) in 2026/27 to £55m (26%) by 2035/36
findings.detail: The HRA is forecast to borrow £848m over the next ten years, primarily £725m for estate regeneration and new housing delivery and £123m for enhanced capital repairs to existing stock. Assuming 50-year repayment periods, interest costs and debt repayment will rise from £17m in the current year to £55m by year ten as the borrowing accumulates. This structural increase in debt service represents a material rise in the proportion of rental income committed to servicing debt.
findings.matters: Rising debt service ratios represent a declining financial resilience and reduced flexibility to manage future cost pressures or tenant affordability constraints. A lender needs to understand whether revenue growth can sustain this debt burden.
findings.figures: £17m (12% of budgeted rental income) in 2026/27, rising to £55m (26%) by 2035/36
findings.quote: The current forecast is that the Council will pay £17m in 2026/27 in interest on borrowing and for the repayment of historic debt. This amounts to 12% of budgeted rental income. By 2035/36, based on the current borrowing projections, this will increase to £55m or 26% of total rental income.

findings.headline: Council recommends phased working-age CTR scheme reform stabilising costs at £7.1m by 2030/31, with implementation from April 2027
findings.detail: The council recommends Option 3, a four-year phased reform beginning April 2027 following consultation. This would stabilise working-age scheme costs at £7.1m annually by 2030/31 through structural changes. The paper notes this option costs more over four years than the faster-saving Option 2 (£40.8m versus £37.4m total) because it reduces hardship risk by moderating impacts through phased implementation.
findings.matters: The council has moved from identifying a budget pressure to implementing a solution with a concrete timeline and financial target; the choice of phased implementation over maximum savings demonstrates managed prioritisation rather than reactive firefighting.
findings.figures: Option 3: £12.5m (2027/28) reducing to £7.1m (2030/31); total 4-year cost £40.8m versus £55.9m under do-nothing
findings.quote: Option 3 delivers structural reform at a sustainable cost while moderating the impact on existing claimants through a less aggressive taper.

findings.headline: Working-age Council Tax Reduction scheme costs projected to reach £14.3m by 2030/31 against £6.9m currently (2026/27)
findings.detail: The council's working-age CTR scheme currently costs £6.9m (2026/27) and represents just over 8% of total council tax income. The council identifies that if council tax increases substantially, maintaining current CTR discount levels would be financially unaffordable. Under the do-nothing scenario, working-age scheme costs would grow to £13.7m (2027/28) and £14.3m (2030/31).
findings.matters: A growing uncontrolled service cost is a key fiscal risk; that the council has identified and quantified this specific pressure demonstrates financial discipline material to lenders assessing the authority's financial control.
findings.figures: Current scheme £6.9m (2026/27); projected under do-nothing scenario £13.7m (2027/28) and £14.3m (2030/31)
findings.quote: Option 1 is considered unsustainable financially for the Council.

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Appendix A3
findings.headline: Council identifies material data gaps on socio-economic status, income, and affordability of non-benefit tenants facing direct increases.
findings.detail: The EINA documents that reliable information is unavailable on household income, employment, affordability, benefit-cap status, and neighbourhood deprivation among affected tenants. Council records on the 3,160 non-benefit tenants provide only whether they have previously engaged with benefits systems, not current entitlement, deductions, or whether increases would be fully met. This limits ability to identify which households may face actual financial hardship.
findings.matters: Incomplete understanding of non-benefit tenants' financial capacity creates risk that arrears could emerge after implementation without sufficient early warning for intervention.
findings.figures: 3,160 tenants without reliable socio-economic data; no data available on income, affordability, or benefit-cap status
findings.quote: No reliable conclusion can currently be drawn about disproportionate impacts on these groups or the ability of households not recorded as receiving housing-related benefits to absorb the increase; these matters are recorded as data gaps.

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Appendix A3
findings.headline: Tenants aged 55+ comprise 60.9% of affected tenancies and 66.6% of non-benefit tenants, potentially facing multi-year convergence periods.
findings.detail: Older tenants are disproportionately represented among affected tenancies, with ages 55+ making up 60.9% of affected tenants versus 53.5% of the overall tenant population. Among affected tenants not receiving benefits, the concentration rises to 66.6%. Older affected tenants are further below formula rent on average and may experience convergence increases for longer periods, with 6,092 tenants (over 61%) facing 6+ years of additional increases.
findings.matters: Risk of non-payment is concentrated in a demographic cohort likely to have fixed or constrained incomes and reduced ability to absorb sustained above-inflation increases.
findings.figures: 55+ comprise 60.9% of affected tenancies, 66.6% of non-benefit cohort; 6,092 (61.1%) are £10+ below formula rent (6+ years to convergence)
findings.quote: Compared with the overall tenant population, older tenants are disproportionately represented among affected tenancies. Tenants aged 55 and over comprise 60.9% of affected tenancies, compared with 53.5% of the overall tenant population. The difference is greater within the affected cohort not believed to receive housing-related benefits, where tenants aged 55 and over comprise 66.6%.

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Appendix A3
findings.headline: 3,160 affected tenants (32%) not receiving housing benefits face direct rent increase exposure with unverified affordability.
findings.detail: Of 9,969 affected tenancies, 6,819 (68%) receive Housing Benefit or Universal Credit housing costs expected to increase with rents. However, 3,160 (32%) are not believed to receive housing-related benefits and will face the additional rent directly. Council records do not establish the affordability of the increase for these households.
findings.matters: A significant minority of affected tenants will face direct rent increases without benefit coverage, creating material arrears risk that could affect HRA income realisation.
findings.figures: 3,160 affected tenants (32%) not believed to receive housing-related benefits; 6,819 (68%) believed to receive benefits
findings.quote: A further 3,160 affected tenants, approximately 32%, are not currently believed to receive housing-related benefits and may therefore face the additional rent directly. Current data does not establish the affordability of the increase for these households.

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Appendix A3
findings.headline: Rent convergence policy permits additional weekly increases to generate HRA income from 9,969 affected tenancies.
findings.detail: The council proposes to adopt the government's rent convergence provision from April 2027, allowing additional weekly increases above the standard annual rent rise for social rent tenancies renting below formula rent. Planning assumptions are £1 per week in 2027/28 and £2 per week from 2028/29 onwards, continuing until affected tenancies reach formula rent.
findings.matters: This is a direct revenue-generation policy designed to support long-term Housing Revenue Account financial sustainability.
findings.figures: 9,969 of approximately 16,550 existing tenancies affected in 2027/28; additional £1/week in 2027/28, £2/week from 2028/29
findings.quote: Current planning assumptions are an additional £1 per week in 2027/28 and £2 per week in subsequent years, continuing until the relevant tenancy reaches formula rent.

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Covering Report
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing identified C3 grading with financial implications
findings.detail: Paper identifies the council's C3 grading from Regulator of Social Housing as a pressure on the HRA, noting it has financial implications, but does not elaborate on grading criteria or specific remedial actions. Listed alongside building safety, damp/mould and inflation as key pressures.
findings.matters: Regulator grades typically signal financial or governance concerns; clarity on remedial actions and timeline would be important to lenders and peer councils.
findings.figures: C3 grading
findings.quote: the financial implications of the Council's C3 grading from the Regulator of Social Housing

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Covering Report
findings.headline: Rent convergence from April 2027 forecast to add £37m to reserves by 2036/37
findings.detail: Business plan assumes maximum rent increases under Government's 10-year rent settlement including rent convergence from April 2027. If fully applied, convergence would affect 9,900 tenants and generate £0.5m additional income in 2027/28 and £1m in 2028/29, with cumulative addition to reserves of £37m by 2036/37. This income is intended to support investment and reduce borrowing reliance.
findings.matters: Key mitigation strategy for managing debt cost trajectory, though dependent on policy implementation and tenant affordability acceptance.
findings.figures: £0.5m additional income 2027/28, £1m 2028/29, £37m total to reserves by 2036/37, 9,900 tenants affected
findings.quote: If applied in full, convergence could affect around 9,900 tenants, generate £0.5m additional income in 2027/28 and a further £1m in 2028/29, generating total addition to reserves of around £37m by 2036/37

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Covering Report
findings.headline: Stock condition survey programme running behind schedule, with target completion December 2026
findings.detail: Council accelerated its stock condition survey with a December 2026 completion target for all tenanted homes and communal surveys. However, progress at August 2026 was behind forecast pace. Emerging survey findings will inform a fully costed asset management and investment strategy, suggesting capital needs may increase.
findings.matters: Schedule slippage on foundational asset assessment risks deferring investment decisions and may reveal larger maintenance liabilities when completed.
findings.figures: Target completion December 2026; survey progress behind forecast at August 2026
findings.quote: The Council has accelerated its stock condition survey programme so that all tenanted homes and communal surveys are completed by December 2026, although progress at August 2026 was behind forecast.

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Covering Report
findings.headline: Building Safety Regulator gateway delays causing capital programme reprofiling and increasing costs
findings.detail: Higher-risk building schemes have had capital cashflows reprofiled due to delays in the Building Safety Regulator's approval process. Median approval times are 35 weeks, and these delays are increasing both consultant fees and contractor costs, creating schedule and budget risk.
findings.matters: Regulatory approval processes beyond the council's control are creating cost pressure and delivery risk on capital investment plans.
findings.figures: 35 weeks (median approval times for Building Safety Regulator gateways)
findings.quote: Capital cashflows have been reprofiled, particularly for higher-risk building schemes affected by Building Safety Regulator gateway delays, with median approval times cited at 35 weeks. These delays are increasing consultant fees and contractor costs.

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Covering Report
findings.headline: Revenue overspends of £7.7m forecast for 2026/27 across repairs, maintenance and management
findings.detail: Forecast for 2026/27 includes overspends of £2.9m on repairs and maintenance, £3.7m on general supervision and management, and £1.1m on special supervision and management. These are partially offset by slippage on external decorations and lower depreciation, but the paper describes continued pressure across operating budgets driven by inflation and safety requirements.
findings.matters: Recurring pressures on controllable costs squeeze headroom available for investment and debt repayment.
findings.figures: £2.9m (repairs/maintenance), £3.7m (general supervision/management), £1.1m (special supervision/management)
findings.quote: the latest forecast for 2026/27 shows continued pressure across operating budgets, including overspends of £2.9m on repairs and maintenance, £3.7m on general supervision and management, and £1.1m on special supervision and management

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Covering Report
findings.headline: £848m HRA borrowing forecast over 10 years: £123m for asset maintenance, £725m for regeneration and new housing
findings.detail: Four-year capital programme totals £662.980m with £325.983m of borrowing. Over 10 years, borrowing is forecast at £848m split between enhanced repairs and improvements to existing stock (£123m) and estate regeneration plus new social housing delivery (£725m). Borrowing is the largest financing element of the capital programme.
findings.matters: Substantial borrowing commitment with multi-decade financial consequences requires careful management of debt sustainability and investment returns.
findings.figures: £848m (10-year borrowing), £123m (repairs/improvements), £725m (regeneration/new housing); £662.980m (4-year capital programme), £325.983m (4-year borrowing)
findings.quote: HRA borrowing of £848m is forecast over the next 10 years, comprising £123m for enhanced capital repairs and improvements to existing stock and £725m for estate regeneration and new social housing delivery

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Covering Report
findings.headline: Debt costs forecast to rise from £17m (12% of rental income) in 2026/27 to £55m (26%) by 2035/36
findings.detail: Planned £848m borrowing over 10 years will drive debt service costs up significantly. By 2035/36, debt costs will consume 26% of rental income, compared to 12% currently. Despite this trajectory, the paper concludes the HRA remains viable.
findings.matters: Rising debt service ratios constrain operating flexibility and increase financial vulnerability; lenders monitor this metric closely.
findings.figures: £17m (2026/27, 12% of rental income); £55m (2035/36, 26% of rental income)
findings.quote: debt costs are forecast to rise from £17m in 2026/27, equivalent to 12% of rental income, to £55m by 2035/36, equivalent to 26% of rental income

findings.paper_title: 26-232 - HRA Business Plan Update - Covering Report
findings.headline: HRA reserves closed at £165.970m in 2025/26, £7.109m below budgeted £173.079m
findings.detail: Reserves opened at £153.273m and closed at £165.970m, falling short of the budget by £7.109m. For 2026/27, the plan assumes reserves will increase to £170.969m, though the paper notes that ongoing pressures on revenue expenditure are likely to challenge this forecast.
findings.matters: Variance of this magnitude shows shortfall against plan and creates downside risk to forward projections.
findings.quote: HRA reserves closed 2025/26 at £165.970m, which was below the expected level

findings.headline: £30.5m of capital receipts planned for Spending Review implementation costs 2026/27-2030/31, including redundancy payments; discovery phase identified £79m of financial benefits
findings.detail: The Council is using the Flexible Use of Capital Receipts flexibility to fund transformation and redundancy costs from a comprehensive Spending Review. An initial £1.9m funded a discovery phase that identified business cases projecting £79m of financial benefits over the MTFS period. A further £29m has been allocated for implementation (£6.9m in 2026/27, £12.6m in 2027/28, £5.4m in 2028/29, £5.6m in 2029/30). The updated flexibility permits all redundancy payments to be capitalised.
findings.matters: Reveals scale and financing of structural change programme; £79m projected benefits need to land for affordability; extends period of transformation investment which signals ongoing pressure on revenue balances.
findings.figures: £30.5m total allocation, £1.9m discovery phase spent, £79m projected benefits, £29m implementation phase funding
findings.quote: An initial budget of £1.9m was allocated to deliver the "discovery" phase of the review, leading to the development of a series of evidence-based business cases that have identified £79m of expected financial benefits over the MTFS period. The ambitious scale of the changes will require further investment in order to successfully deliver this benefit and £29m of funding has been allocated to cover the cost of the implementation phase.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered at only 77% of budget in 2025/26; £29.6m slippage carried forward with major items: Nine Elms Park (£10m), Wandsworth Town Station (£2.6m), Battersea River Wall (£1.5m)
findings.detail: The Council's capital programme is facing delivery delays. Outturn in 2025/26 was £93.7m against a revised budget of £121.4m (22.8% underspend), with £29.6m of planned spending carried forward to future years. Major slippage items include Nine Elms Park (developer-led completion delays), Wandsworth Town Station improvements (Network Rail delivery schedule), and Battersea River Wall stabilisation (complex specialist works requiring marine civil engineers).
findings.matters: Shows capital programme not being delivered at planned pace; impacts timing of borrowing, revenue financing costs, and indicates delivery/partnership challenges that a lender monitoring cash flow and debt serviceability would need to track.
findings.figures: Outturn £93.7m vs revised budget £121.4m (underspend £27.7m); slippage £29.6m; Nine Elms £10m, Wandsworth Town Station £2.6m, Battersea River Wall £1.5m
findings.quote: Nine Elms Park (£10 million) project is led by the external developers, and the payments are made at trigger points of completion of the works. Site completion delays mean that payments will be made later than expected. Wandsworth Town Station - Access to all (£2.6 million). Works started late February 2026 and are being delivered by Network Rail.

findings.headline: Net Zero Decarbonisation (£20m), Town Centre Transformation (£18m) and Alton Renewal (£9.5m) budgets removed or substantially reduced
findings.detail: The Spending Review has scaled back or removed major environmental and regeneration schemes. The Net Zero Decarbonisation Strategy (£20m) and Environment/Sustainability Strategy (£8.2m) funding has been released to be reallocated to housing stock improvements (responding to C3 energy rating). The Town Centre Transformation (£18m) has been revised to lower-cost proposals pending TfL's consultation. Alton Estate Renewal (£9.5m) is being reviewed to focus on Block A and co-locate community services.
findings.matters: Deprioritisation of environmental and regeneration schemes signals changed strategic focus; may affect external funding partnerships and regeneration timescales that lenders are tracking.
findings.figures: £20m Net Zero Decarbonisation, £8.2m Sustainability Strategy, £18m Town Centre Transformation, £9.5m Alton Renewal
findings.quote: Net Zero Decarbonisation Strategy (£20 million) and Wandsworth Environment and Sustainability Strategy (£8.2 million). The Council will release unallocated funds previously earmarked for the delivery of the decarbonisation and environment and sustainability strategies for allocation elsewhere until specific schemes are identified.

findings.headline: Capital programme reduced from £350.3m to £313.2m through removal of £77.9m uncommitted schemes; borrowing requirement cut by £33.7m
findings.detail: The new administration's Spending Review has removed or reduced uncommitted capital schemes totalling £77.9m, while adding only £6m in new priorities. This generates a £33.7m reduction in the borrowing requirement, which will lower future revenue financing costs. The revised programme totals £313.2m over the five-year period.
findings.matters: Shows change in administration priorities and improves medium-term affordability by reducing borrowing costs, a key indicator of financial health for any council and its lenders.
findings.figures: £77.9m reductions, £6.0m additions, £33.7m borrowing reduction, revised programme £313.2m
findings.quote: proposed additions of £3.0 million to the capital programme, alongside the removal or reduction of uncommitted schemes totalling £77.9 million. Taken together with the application of available financing resources, these changes reduce the Council's borrowing requirement by £33.7 million

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation subsidy cap creates growing unfunded pressure as government subsidy frozen at 2011 Local Housing Allowance rates while rents continue rising.
findings.detail: For housing benefit paid to temporary accommodation households, government subsidy is capped at January 2011 Local Housing Allowance rates and is not reimbursing councils for the actual cost of securing accommodation. This cap has not kept pace with real costs, particularly in high-rent inner London. As homelessness demand rises and households spend longer in temporary accommodation, the gap between what councils pay providers and what they can recover via housing benefit subsidy grows automatically. The council notes measures to reduce demand and costs will 'take time to deliver and cannot fully offset the wider national and London housing pressures'.
findings.matters: This is an unfunded mandate. The gap widens automatically as rents rise and homelessness pressures increase. No current government support exists to close it. It is a permanent structural cost on the council for a service driven by national policy and housing market factors beyond its control.
findings.figures: Capped at January 2011 Local Housing Allowance rates (no current rates provided in paper)
findings.quote: For housing benefit paid to households in temporary accommodation the Government's subsidy...is limited to the relevant Local Housing Allowance rate in January 2011. This has not kept pace with the real cost of securing accommodation...The MTFS therefore assumes that homelessness and temporary accommodation will remain a significant financial risk

findings.headline: HRA to borrow £326m over four-year framework to fund repairs, fire safety and stock condition work; rent convergence policy change to support borrowing costs.
findings.detail: The HRA business plan update (reported separately to Housing Committee) shows the HRA faces pressures from repairs budget, fire safety commitments, issues following regulatory inspection and stock condition survey findings. To support the current plans the HRA will need to borrow £326m over the four-year framework period. The proposed amendment to rent policy will allow rent convergence via the annual rent-setting decision, generating additional income to support increased investment in repairs and maintenance and to service this borrowing.
findings.matters: £326m is substantial borrowing for the ringfenced HRA. It increases future debt servicing cost but is justified by the need to meet Awaab's Law and regulatory stock condition standards. This is capital investment borrowing for a revenue-producing asset, but the scale signals the degree of catch-up investment needed on the stock.
findings.figures: £326m borrowing over four-year framework period
findings.quote: To support current plans there would need to be borrowing of £326m over the four year framework period

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Budget deficit: government writes off 90% (£30m), council funds 10% (£3.3m) plus potential £6.7m for 2026/27–27/28 deficits.
findings.detail: The Council's Dedicated Schools Budget faces a deficit due to SEND overspends. Government High Needs Stability Grant will write off 90% of accumulated DSB deficit as at 31 March 2026, approximately £30m for Wandsworth. The council must fund the remaining 10%, estimated at £3.3m. Government has not yet confirmed support for deficits accumulating in 2026/27 and 2027/28, but has committed to 'an appropriate and proportionate approach but it will not be unlimited'; the council has estimated a further £6.7m could need to be funded from General Fund reserves.
findings.matters: The £3.3m immediate cost is material. The £6.7m estimate for future years is unquantified government exposure. The language 'not unlimited' signals government is setting a ceiling on its support, placing further cost risk on the council.
findings.figures: £30m (90% government write-off), £3.3m (10% council funds), potentially £6.7m additional
findings.quote: The Council will therefore have to fund the remaining 10%, estimated to be £3.3m...An estimate of £6.7m has been built into plans to fund the Council portion

findings.headline: Council identifies £79m of ongoing savings by 2030/31 but paper explicitly states 'Delivery of savings at this scale carries significant risk'.
findings.detail: The Spending Review proposes £79m of ongoing savings by 2030/31. The council acknowledges these savings reduce the budget gap but do not close it entirely. The paper states that delivery 'will require strong programme governance, clear accountability and regular monitoring to ensure corrective action is taken where savings are not delivered in full or on time.' A delivery plan is included as Appendix 3 and requires significant upfront one-off investment on an invest-to-save basis.
findings.matters: Savings of this magnitude carry material delivery risk. If delayed or not achieved in full, the council would need to draw reserves further, increase charges, cut services or reduce capital investment beyond current plans. The council's own language signals this is a high-bar target.
findings.figures: £79m ongoing savings by 2030/31; £29m reserve allocation to support delivery of savings
findings.quote: Delivery of savings at this scale carries significant risk and will require strong programme governance, clear accountability and regular monitoring to ensure corrective action is taken where savings are not delivered in full or on time

findings.headline: 2025/26 General Fund overspent by £9.8m with adult social care (£3.5m) and children's services (£4m) continuing to overspend.
findings.detail: The council's net General Fund expenditure overspent by £9.8m in 2025/26. Adult social care is forecast to overspend by £3.5m in the current year driven by increasing demand, greater complexity of need and care market pressures; councils nationally are overspending adult social care by £715m. Children's social care is projecting an overspend of £4m, with main areas of pressure from children looked after, children with disabilities, SEND transport costs and placement market strain.
findings.matters: These are demand-led services where the council has statutory duties. The overspends are recurring and growing. The paper acknowledges them as 'significant financial risks' going forward, signalling that current mitigation plans will not fully eliminate pressure.
findings.figures: £9.8m General Fund overspend 2025/26; £3.5m adult social care forecast overspend; £4m children's services overspend; £715m national adult social care overspend 2025/26
findings.quote: the 2025/26 outturn position where the Council's net General Fund expenditure overspent by £9.8m...budgets are forecast to overspend by £3.5m in the current year...An overspend of £4m is currently being projected

findings.headline: General Fund reserves depleted from £205m (2023) to projected £76m minimum by end of four-year MTFS period.
findings.detail: Reserve balances have fallen from £205m in 2023 to £162m at the start of 2026/27 and are projected to drop below £100m by year end. Under current modelling, balances could reach around £76m by the end of the four-year period, which the council identifies as the minimum level needed to retain financial resilience. Planning to drop below this level would leave the council financially exposed.
findings.matters: This trajectory shows the council is using reserves as a bridge while it implements permanent solutions. A reserve of £76m on a budget of this size represents minimal buffer against delivery delays, demand spikes, or inflation above forecast. The council is foreclosing its options to absorb further shocks.
findings.figures: £205m (2023), £162m (start 2026/27), projected below £100m by year end, £76m minimum by end of four-year period
findings.quote: Reserve balances have reduced from a high of £205m in 2023 to £162m at the start of 2026/27 and are projected to fall below £100m by the end of the year...balances could reduce to around £76m over the four year period, which is the minimum level needed to retain financial resilience

findings.headline: Council tax planned to rise from £510 to £1,468 (Band D) in 2027/28 — a 94% increase — to help close the structural budget gap.
findings.detail: The Spending Review concludes the council must combine savings, service reform, income generation, capital reductions, controlled reserve use and a significant council tax increase to restore sustainability. The planning assumption for council's share of Band D is an increase from £510 to £1,468 in 2027/28. Including the Greater London Authority precept, the total Band D bill would be approximately £1,978. Decisions will be taken by Full Council in March 2027, but residents are being given notice because of the scale of potential increase.
findings.matters: A 94% increase is unprecedented for most councils and indicates the severity of Wandsworth's position. It shows the council has exhausted other options and is explicitly asking residents to pay materially more. It also signals whether the tax base can absorb such an increase without creating demand management issues of its own.
findings.figures: Band D council's share £510 to £1,468; total with GLA precept approximately £1,978; 94% increase
findings.quote: the Council should plan on the basis of its share of Band D council tax increasing from £510 to £1,468 in 2027/28...which is a 94% increase on the current year's charge

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review causes £84m annual loss of core government funding by 2028/29 — a 40% cut, the largest loss in the country.
findings.detail: Wandsworth was one of six authorities protected only by the 95% funding guarantee under the Fair Funding Review, equivalent to a 5% cash cut. The authority will lose £19m of funding in 2026/27 rising to £84m per year by 2028/29. This loss is structural and permanent; it reflects redistribution away from authorities with historically low council tax and strong tax bases.
findings.matters: A 40% grant loss is existential. It is not a temporary pressure but a permanent reduction that cannot be funded by normal efficiency savings or temporary measures; the council has explicitly said it requires council tax increases, reserve drawdown, and fundamental service changes.
findings.figures: £19m in 2026/27 rising to £84m per year by 2028/29; 40% cut; 95% funding guarantee (5% cash reduction)
findings.quote: the Council is set to lose £19m of funding in 2026/27 rising to £84m per year by 2028/29, a 40% cut

findings.headline: National pay award of 3.3% exceeds budgeted provision of 2.5%, creating £1.2m pressure on contingency
findings.detail: The national local government pay award finalised in July 2026 at 3.3% is higher than the 2.5% provision made when setting the 2026/27 budget. This variance has not yet been reflected in individual service budgets and is creating a £1.2m pressure on the council's inflation contingency reserve. The contingency was set at £15.362m based on expected inflation of 2.8%.
findings.matters: An inflation contingency already containing only limited headroom above expected inflation is now reduced by an unfunded pay award, constraining the council's ability to manage other in-year price pressures.
findings.figures: 3.3% actual pay award vs 2.5% budgeted, £1.2m contingency pressure, contingency budget £15.362m
findings.quote: The national local government pay award has been finalised in July at a 3.3% increase. This is not yet reflected in service budgets and is higher than the provision (2.5%) allowed for when the budget was set leading to a pressure on the contingency of £1.2m.

findings.headline: Treasury position better than budget due to internal borrowing capability and higher investment income
findings.detail: Finance OSC shows a £0.688m underspend in Treasury. The budget assumed external borrowing would be required, but this has been confirmed as unnecessary — all borrowing needs can be met from internal resources, eliminating planned external interest payments. Additionally, interest earned on cash balances is expected to exceed budget due to elevated interest rate environment.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing capability is a significant strategic advantage for a council, reducing both cost of capital and refinancing risk; higher investment income improves the fiscal position.
findings.figures: £0.688m Treasury underspend forecast
findings.quote: the budget was set using the most prudent assumption around borrowing externally which it is confirmed can be met internally and hence no external interest payments are due. Due to global events, interest rates remain high and there is also a possible rate increase in year. Interest earned on cash balances is therefore expected to be higher than budgeted for.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account forecast surplus of £11.7m in year with closing balance of £152.658m
findings.detail: The HRA is performing significantly better than the general fund. The HRA is forecast to produce a £11.7m surplus in 2026/27 and a closing revenue balance of £152.658m. Overspends in repairs and maintenance (£2.9m) and supervision and management (£3.7m and £1.1m) are offset by slippage on external decorations (£5.8m), lower than anticipated depreciation (£1.8m), and rental income £1.8m above budget. This demonstrates robust rental income performance despite general fund pressures.
findings.matters: The HRA's strong reserve position and in-year surplus provides counterbalance to general fund pressures and demonstrates that the rental income base is performing robustly.
findings.figures: £11.7m surplus forecast, £152.658m closing balance, repairs overspend £2.9m, decorations slippage £5.8m
findings.quote: Overall, the most recent revenue forecast is showing an £11.7m surplus in year and a forecast closing revenue balance of £152.658m.

findings.headline: Waste disposal costs remain above budget despite substantial increase in recycling volumes
findings.detail: Environment OSC forecasts a near breakeven position, but this depends on £1.099m of mitigating actions. Waste & Recycling shows a pressure due to residual waste tonnages remaining above budget. The council's food waste collection rollout and recycling expansion were designed to shift waste to lower-cost disposal streams, but although recycling volumes have substantially increased, residual waste volumes remain high. Costs are being managed through grant-funded reserves.
findings.matters: A service expansion expected to generate savings through modal shift (waste to recycling) has not produced the anticipated benefit, indicating a gap between policy design and cost outcome that may affect future decisions.
findings.figures: £1.099m mitigating actions required for breakeven forecast
findings.quote: Whilst recycling volumes have substantially increased, the levels within the residual waste stream remains in excess of budget.

findings.headline: Children's social care overspend of £5.04m on placements and £1.9m on SEN transport amid growing complexity
findings.detail: Children's Services forecasts a £1.160m overall overspend, but within this, social care is forecasting a £5.04m overspend on residential and homecare provision for children looked after and children with disabilities. SEN transport is overspending by £1.9m due to continued growth in Education, Health and Care Plans and increasing complexity. These pressures are partially offset by utilising grant income (£3.56m). The forecast carries explicit risk that needs increase further, as has happened in previous years.
findings.matters: Placement and SEN transport pressures are widespread across councils; Wandsworth's specific forecast and explicit risk flagging shows the scale of the challenge and dependency on offsetting grant income.
findings.figures: £1.160m Children's overspend forecast, £5.04m social care placements, £1.9m SEN transport, £3.56m grant-funded offset, £3.179m mitigating actions required
findings.quote: Children's social care is forecasting a £5.04m overspend position. This is due to the costs of residential provision for Children Looked After continuing to rise as well as the increased cost of homecare packages for children with disabilities. There is also a £1.9m overspend forecast on SEN transport where there has been a continued increase in the number of children with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), alongside greater complexity of need.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation numbers grew 188 cases in Q1 to 5,005, with intake-to-move ratio currently 10 in for every 1 out
findings.detail: The number of people housed in temporary accommodation or owed statutory homelessness duty grew from 4,817 at the start of the year to 5,005 at Q1 end, a net growth of 188 cases. The council describes the current ratio as 10 people entering TA for every 1 person leaving. The paper states the council needs to stabilise numbers and achieve significant net reduction to bring the service back into budget. The forecast depends on fundamental reshaping of the practice model and changing the ratio to 3 in for every 10 out.
findings.matters: Growing demand for temporary accommodation is a material budget pressure; a council stating that demand is currently flowing in the wrong direction and that major service transformation is needed indicates a significant operational and financial risk.
findings.figures: 5,005 cases at Q1 end (up from 4,817), 188 net growth in Q1, current intake-to-move ratio 10:1, £4.6m mitigating actions required
findings.quote: Current overall numbers housed in TA or assessed as owed statutory homelessness duty as at the end of Q1 was 5,005 compared to a start of year position of 4,817, a growth of 188 cases. Currently 10 people come into temporary accommodation for every 1 that leaves.

findings.headline: Adult social care overspend of £3.477m driven by unfunded demographic growth and increasing complexity of need
findings.detail: Health OSC is forecasting an overspend of £3.477m, primarily in Adult Social Care. The paper attributes this to unfunded demographic growth and increasing complexity of need, particularly in services for older people and adults with learning disabilities. The forecast includes £1.630m of future demand growth, of which £1.001m relates to children's care packages transitioning to Adult Social Care. Delivery of mitigating actions depends on assessments and reviews.
findings.matters: Unfunded demographic growth in social care is a structural pressure facing councils; quantified examples of the gap between statutory demand and available funding are material to credit assessments.
findings.figures: £3.477m Adult Social Care overspend, £1.630m future demand growth forecast, £1.001m from children transitioning to adult services, £0.608m mitigating actions planned
findings.quote: This position is primarily driven by Adult Social Care demand pressures, mainly relating to Services for Older People, Sensory and Physical Disabilities and Services for Adults with Learning Disabilities. This is reflecting underlying unfunded demographic growth and increasing complexity of need, particularly in services for older people and adults with learning disabilities.

findings.headline: General Fund projected to overspend by £5.306m at Q1 2026/27, dependent on £12m mitigating actions
findings.detail: The council is forecasting an overspend of £5.306m (1.7%) against a budget of £311.203m. This forecast assumes delivery of £12m of mitigating actions across services. The council had already added £16.9m to the budget when setting the 2026/27 position to recognise known service pressures, yet remains in deficit. If mitigating actions do not land, the overspend will increase.
findings.matters: A material forecast overspend that depends entirely on successful delivery of planned actions represents a significant risk to the council's in-year outturn and places pressure on reserves.
findings.figures: £5.306m overspend (1.7% of £311.203m budget), £12m mitigating actions assumed, £16.9m added to budget for known pressures
findings.quote: The Council is currently projecting an overspend of £5.306m (or 1.7%) compared to the approved General Fund revenue budget of £311.203m as at Q1. This forecast position assumes the in-year delivery of a total of £12m of mitigating actions.

findings.headline: Pension contribution rate reduced from 19.1% to 15.5% following improved fund valuation.
findings.detail: The Wandsworth Pension Fund's most recent actuarial valuation (31 March 2025) reported an overall funding level of 121%, improved from 116% at the previous valuation in 2022. Wandsworth Council's individual employer funding level improved from 131% to 135.9%. As a result, the overall employer contribution rate has reduced from 19.1% to 15.5% of pensionable pay for the three years from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2029.
findings.matters: This is a significant cost relief on the council's payroll during a period of severe financial pressure. The next valuation is due 31 March 2028, with revised rates taking effect 1 April 2029.
findings.figures: Funding level 121% (up from 116%); contribution rate 15.5% (down from 19.1%)
findings.quote: the overall employer contribution rate for the Council has reduced from 19.1% to 15.5% of pensionable pay for the three year period commencing 1 April 2026 and ending 31 March 2029

findings.headline: Pay inflation surprise: 3.3% award agreed against 2.5% budget, creating £1.2m ongoing overspend.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 national pay award for Council staff was agreed at 3.3%, whereas the budget had assumed 2.5%. This causes an immediate overspend pressure of £1.2m per year ongoing. The paper notes that increases in National Minimum Wage, London Living Wage and continuing impact of employers' national insurance contributions will continue to put above-inflation pressure on contractors' costs.
findings.matters: Shows the council's budget assumptions can be overtaken by external factors beyond its control. The 0.8% variance on pay creates £1.2m recurring cost. Contractor cost inflation continues to exceed general inflation.
findings.figures: 3.3% pay award versus 2.5% budgeted; £1.2m per year ongoing overspend
findings.quote: The 2026/27 pay award for Council staff has recently been agreed nationally at 3.3% whereas the budget assumed 2.5%, causing an immediate overspend pressure of £1.2m per year ongoing

findings.headline: Homelessness subsidy cap creating growing unfunded pressure as gap widens.
findings.detail: The Government's subsidy for Housing Benefit paid to households in temporary accommodation is limited to the Local Housing Allowance rate from January 2011, which has not kept pace with actual accommodation costs. As homelessness demand rises, households spend longer in temporary accommodation, and rents increase, the gap between what the council pays providers and what it can recover via subsidy grows. The council is taking action to manage demand through prevention, private rented sector discharge and out-of-borough placements, but these measures will take time to deliver.
findings.matters: This is a structural unfunded pressure that will persist and potentially grow if homelessness demand continues to rise. The council's recovery is limited by a fixed subsidy cap from 2011, while London rents have increased significantly since then.
findings.figures: Subsidy capped at January 2011 LHA levels
findings.quote: For housing benefit paid to households in temporary accommodation the Government's subsidy (reimbursement of the housing benefit paid out) back to councils is limited to the relevant Local Housing Allowance rate in January 2011

findings.headline: Children's social care overspend of £4m, driven by placement costs and SEND transport.
findings.detail: An overspend of £4m is projected in children's social care in 2025/26, despite Wandsworth's Children's Services being rated Outstanding by Ofsted in May 2026. Main pressures are rising complexity of need for children looked after and with disabilities, and transport costs from growth in SEND demand. The council is addressing this through early help and prevention, increasing local provision and improving placement commissioning, but these measures will take time to deliver.
findings.matters: Like adult social care, this is a demand-led budget where the council faces pressures from demographic and market factors beyond its control. A Good/Outstanding rating does not protect the budget from cost pressures.
findings.figures: £4m projected overspend
findings.quote: An overspend of £4m is currently being projected in this financial year

findings.headline: Adult social care overspend of £3.5m forecast despite service rated Good by CQC.
findings.detail: Wandsworth's adult social care is rated Good by the Care Quality Commission, but budgets are forecast to overspend by £3.5m in the current year. The paper attributes this to increasing demand, greater complexity of need and sustained care market pressures. The council is implementing initiatives including digital technology, integrated neighbourhood health and care, and strategic mental health commissioning to manage demand and improve efficiency.
findings.matters: Adult social care is one of the largest areas of council expenditure and remains a significant financial risk. Overspends persist even in a Good-rated service, suggesting demand and complexity are outstripping capacity and efficiency measures.
findings.figures: £3.5m projected overspend
findings.quote: budgets are forecast to overspend by £3.5m in the current year

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Budget deficit: Council to fund £3.3m plus potentially £6.7m more.
findings.detail: The DSB faces significant pressures from SEND overspends. The Government's High Needs Stability Grant will write off 90% of the accumulated deficit as at 31 March 2026 (approximately £30m for Wandsworth), but the Council must fund the remaining 10%, estimated at £3.3m. For future deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28, Government support is unconfirmed; the council has estimated an additional £6.7m may need to be funded from General Fund reserves.
findings.matters: This represents an unfunded pressure on the General Fund from a demand-led, ringfenced budget. The council has limited control over SEND placement costs and demand. Additional £6.7m risk could materialise.
findings.figures: £3.3m (10% of accumulated deficit); £6.7m estimated for 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits; accumulated deficit approximately £30m
findings.quote: The Council will therefore have to fund the remaining 10%, estimated to be £3.3m

findings.headline: HRA planned borrowing of £326m over four years to fund housing repairs and development.
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account (HRA), which manages 33,200 council housing properties on a ringfenced basis, is planning borrowing of £326m over the four-year framework period. This borrowing is needed to fund repairs and maintenance (including fire safety commitments and addressing stock condition survey issues) and investment in housing development and regeneration. The HRA revenue forecast shows a closing balance of £153m plus £25m of capital reserves.
findings.matters: This is significant new borrowing on top of the General Fund's financial pressures. For a lender, it shows the council's total borrowing trajectory and whether the HRA can service this new debt from rental income.
findings.figures: £326m HRA borrowing over four years; closing revenue balance £153m plus £25m capital reserves
findings.quote: an assumed level of borrowing of £326m over the four year framework period

findings.headline: General Fund borrowing reduced by £39m, avoiding £2.3m annual debt servicing costs.
findings.detail: The Spending Review has removed £39m of future General Fund borrowing from the planned capital programme, avoiding an estimated £2.3m of revenue debt servicing costs over four years. The capital programme has been reprioritised to focus on essential, affordable and deliverable schemes; lower priority schemes have been stopped, reduced or reshaped.
findings.matters: Shows the council is prioritising affordability by reducing new borrowing commitments and making hard choices about capital schemes. This protects the council's future revenue budget from long-term debt servicing costs.
findings.figures: £39m borrowing reduction; £2.3m revenue debt servicing cost saving over four years
findings.quote: The Spending Review has removed £39m of future General Fund borrowing, avoiding an estimated £2.3m of revenue debt servicing costs over the next four years

findings.headline: £79m of ongoing savings targeted by 2030/31, with significant delivery risk acknowledged.
findings.detail: The Spending Review identifies ambitious plans to deliver £79m of ongoing savings by 2030/31 across all areas of spending. These savings reduce but do not remove the budget gap. The paper acknowledges that delivery of savings at this scale carries significant risk and will require strong programme governance, clear accountability and regular monitoring. £29m of reserves has been allocated to fund the transformation investment needed (invest-to-save basis).
findings.matters: Savings of this scale are difficult to deliver and often slip. If not achieved on time or in full, the council will need to use more reserves or make difficult in-year cuts. For a lender, this represents a key delivery risk to the financial plan.
findings.figures: £79m ongoing savings by 2030/31; £29m reserve investment for transformation
findings.quote: Spending Review identifies ambitious plans to deliver £79m of ongoing savings by 2030/31

findings.headline: Reserves projected to decline to £76m—the minimum level needed to retain financial resilience.
findings.detail: Reserve balances have fallen from £205m in 2023 to £162m at the start of 2026/27 and are forecast to fall below £100m by year end. Current modelling indicates balances could reduce to around £76m by end of the MTFS period (2030/31), described as the minimum needed to maintain financial resilience. The council has allocated £29m of available reserves to a Spending Review Delivery Fund for invest-to-save initiatives.
findings.matters: A sharp reserve depletion reduces the council's financial buffer to absorb shocks. If reserves fall below £76m, the council would be financially exposed and unable to adjust to changes in circumstances. For a lender, this shows limited headroom for unexpected costs or if savings fail to materialise.
findings.figures: £205m (2023); £162m (start 2026/27); projected below £100m by end of year; £76m minimum by 2030/31; £29m allocated to Spending Review Delivery Fund
findings.quote: reserve balances have reduced from a high of £205m in 2023 to £162m at the start of 2026/27 and are projected to fall below £100m by the end of the year
